newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Turkmenistan puts hopes of recovery on gas exports.
newsitem.headline: Turkmenistan puts hopes of recovery on gas exports.

text.p: Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov said on Wednesday he was pinning hopes for the economic revival of his impoverished desert nation on renewed exports of natural gas to western Europe.
Niyazov said on state television the former Soviet republic would nearly double gas exports in 1997 to 40 billion cubic metres (bcm) (1.413 trillion cu ft) from 24 bcm this year.
Half of those exports will be directed to west European consumers who can pay with desperately needed hard currency.
Niyazov said the gas sales would allow his cash-strapped government to spend more.

The docile Turkmen parliament will examine a new draft budget behind closed doors on Friday. But Niyazov's attempts to continue a Soviet-style welfare state, including free energy and low-cost food to the 3.8 million population, have largely backfired.
Turkmenistan saw revenues shrivel when Russia stopped Turkmen gas going to western Europe in 1993 and diverted it to other hard-up former Soviet republics.

The republic is constructing a gas pipeline to neighbouring Iran and there are plans to build an export pipeline to Pakistan via war-ravaged Afghanistan. But for now, the republic is completely beholden to its former colonial master.

"In 1997, in agreement with (Russia's) Gazprom, 20 billion cubic metres of natural gas will be exported to Europe," Niyazov said. Recent gas production figures are not available but output in 1994 was just over half Soviet-era levels of 64 bcm.
The 1996 cotton crop, another important hard currency earner, was disastrous. Just 430,000 tonnes of raw cotton was harvested, far below last year's 1.3 million tonnes.
An unusually candid report on tightly-controlled state television on Tuesday blamed the poor harvest on the large backlog of unpaid salaries to cotton workers.

A Soviet-style plan to make the republic self-sufficient in grains this year also failed. The 400,000-tonne harvest was far below last year's 1.0 million tonnes and a government target of 1.2 million.
Niyazov, the self-styled "leader of the Turkmens" who has built up a strong personality cult, lashed out at officials on Tuesday over the poor harvest.
"Turkmenistan has never worked so badly," he said on television. "We have no further choice -- either we starve or we fulfil the self-sufficiency programme."
Turkmens, whose salaries average about $10 a month if they are paid at all, are already going hungry.
Prices for subsidised bread were doubled earlier this month to 400 manats (eight cents), while traditional flat loaves in private markets go for more than three times that price.

Earlier this year, Turkmens poured into the capital Ashgabat from the poverty-stricken regions in the hope of finding bread to buy. But a massive hike in transport costs has almost halted the flow and led to a scarcity of fresh food from small-scale traders in Ashgabat itself.
State television said this week a lack of feed grains has seen 20 percent of Turkmenistan's livestock die in 1996.
Gas revenues might allow Niyazov to carry on with his state-led economic policies. But patience in the republic, which borders Iran east of the Caspian Sea, is running out.

"Our energy reserves will just seep into the sand under this system," said a disillusioned scientist queueing to buy bread in Ashgabat on Wednesday. "Ten Kuwaits will not be enough for this government," he said. ($1 = about 5,000 manats)
